parts.description: A balloon whisk with thin polished stainless-steel wire loops, a coiled metal collar, and a smooth light wood handle with a small hanging loop.
parts.reasoning: Estimated as a medium kitchen balloon whisk approximately 0.30-0.32 m long, with a 0.075-0.09 m diameter wire bulb, a 0.13-0.15 m wooden handle around 25 mm in diameter, and 1.2-1.6 mm stainless wires. The handle volume is roughly 5.5e-5 to 7.0e-5 m3; at 600-750 kg/m3 for beech/maple-like wood this contributes about 35-50 g. The stainless wire loops, collar coil, and hanging loop contribute roughly 45-70 g depending on wire count and diameter, giving a practical total mass estimate near 0.115 kg. The density value is an aggregate solid-volume density for the mixed wood/steel construction, not a bounding-box density; if authoring separate materials, use about 650 kg/m3 for the wood handle and 7850 kg/m3 for the stainless steel while keeping the explicit mass override. The dominant exposed structural/contact surface is polished stainless steel wire, with the wood handle as a significant secondary surface, so friction is set between typical steel and dry wood contact values: moderate static friction and slightly lower dynamic friction. Restitution is kept moderate-low because the wooden handle and thin wire assembly dissipate energy even though stainless steel alone would be bouncier. For collision, a single convex hull is not recommended because it would fill the open whisk cage and produce unrealistic contacts. A compound convex decomposition is preferred: one or several convex pieces for the handle and collar, plus simplified slender convex/capsule-like hulls for the wire loops and hook. SDF mesh collision can preserve the exact wire openings, but it is more expensive and may jitter on sub-2 mm wires unless resolution is high. CCD is enabled because the wire radius is very small and tunneling can occur during drops, impacts, or fast grasping. A 2 mm contact offset gives reliable early contact generation for thin features without excessively inflating the utensil; rest offset is left at zero for visual/collision alignment. For stable Isaac Sim v4.5 behavior, use explicit mass and preferably explicit inertia/COM if available; the center of mass should lie closer to the collar/handle than the geometric center of the full whisk. For high-speed tests, cap linear velocity around 5-10 m/s and angular velocity around 40-60 rad/s, and use low sleep thresholds so the light object settles without premature hibernation. Compliant contacts are disabled because this is treated as a rigid, non-deformable asset.
